"If atoms are unestablished in their own nature, then what do you establish?" When the own-nature is unestablished, an entity is not established; therefore our position is established. One does not even accidentally say that atoms have a many-nature; when the atom is unestablished, how could many-nature be appropriate?—this is what I have said. Those atoms that you establish as partless, since they are accepted as having the divisions of directional parts such as east, west, and the like, they are accepted as having the division of directional parts; therefore they absurdly become possessing parts. From that, the unestablishedness of the basis of the reason is established through the absurd consequence. And they are not merely inconclusive because of mind and mental factors, since those, being formless (<s>amūrta</s>), do not abide in directions and do not persist in eastern, western, and other directions either.

body.text: tenoktam-
body.translated_text: Therefore it has been said:

children.text: na rūpe naiva netre ca tayormadhye 'pi na sthitaḥ |
children.translated_text: "Not in form and not in the eye, nor established in between the two,

children.text: yatra sthito bhavettatra na sannaiva hi cāpyasat ||
children.translated_text: Where it would abide, there it is neither existent nor indeed non-existent."

body.text: alaṃ prasaṅgeneti | anena tvanekasvabhāvarāhityamavagamya nirābhāsopāyasandarśanena yogasamāpattiścittaprahaśceti nirdiṣṭam | bahuḥ sa paramāṇusañcayo bhavet ityanenaudāryaṃ cābhihitam, avaśeṣeṇa tu gāmbhīryam |
body.translated_text: Enough with digressions. By this, having comprehended the absence of many-nature and through the demonstration of the method of eliminating appearance, <s>yogasamāpatti</s> (meditative attainment) and the uplift of the mind (<s>cittapragraha</s>) have been indicated. By "Would that aggregation of atoms be much," the vastness has also been stated; by the remainder, the profundity.

body.text: (ba) sattvalokādhipatyena prasthitiḥ
body.translated_text: (b) The setting-forth through mastery over the sentient-being world

body.text: samprati sattvalokābhāvaprasthitimadhikṛtya bhāṣitastrisāhasramahāsāhasro lokadhāturiti saḥ ityādyāha | bhājanalokasya pūrvamuktatvādatra lokadhātustāvat sattvalokatveneṣṭaḥ | ubhayatra trisāhasramahāsāhasrābhidhānena tāvadanantalokadhāturupalakṣyate | ata eva adhātuḥ sa tathāgatena bhāṣitaḥ iti pañcaskandhātmakaḥ sa sattvaloko 'pyekānekasvabhāvavirahitaḥ pūrvavaduktaḥ |
body.translated_text: Now, addressing the setting-forth through the non-existence of the sentient-being world, since "the three-thousand-great-thousand world-system" was stated, he says "that" and so forth. Since the vessel-world has already been stated, here the "world-system" is intended as the sentient-being world. In both cases, by the designation "three-thousand-great-thousand," infinite world-realms are indicated. For this very reason, "that is spoken of by the <s>Tathāgata</s> as non-realm" means: that sentient-being world, consisting of the five <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates), is also devoid of one-and-many nature, as stated previously.

body.text: anena tathāgatasya tathāvidhāyāṃ sattvalokābhāvaprasthitau bodhisattvena chandapraṇidhānābhyāṃ sthātavyamiti nirdiṣṭam | nirābhāsena tu yogasamāpattiriyaṃ kathaṃ pratipattavyetyapi sandarśitam |
body.translated_text: By this, it is indicated that a <s>bodhisattva</s> should abide in the <s>Tathāgata</s>'s setting-forth through the non-existence of the sentient-being world through aspiration (<s>chanda</s>) and resolve (<s>praṇidhāna</s>). And through the elimination of appearance, how this <s>yogasamāpatti</s> should be practiced has also been demonstrated.

body.text: idānīṃ cittaṃ kathaṃ pragrahītavyamiti darśayituṃ tatkasya hetoḥ? iti pṛṣṭavān | 'adhātuḥ sa tathāgatena bhāṣita'; ityanena yojanīyam | uttarārthaṃ saced bhagavan ityādyāha | yadi sattvaloko yathāprasiddhastathā paramārthataḥ syāt sthūlaikasvabhāvastadā tathāgatena yathāsthiti vastutattvamadhigatamiti sa eva (

children.translated_text: [<s>Vajraṭ</s> 221]
Would be an aggregate-grasping (<s>piṇḍagrāha</s>).

body.translated_text: Now, in order to show how the mind should be uplifted, he asked "For what reason?" This should be connected with "that is spoken of by the <s>Tathāgata</s> as non-realm." For the purpose of the subsequent meaning, he says "If, <s>Bhagavān</s>" and so forth. If the sentient-being world existed ultimately just as it is commonly known, with a gross unitary nature, then the <s>Tathāgata</s>'s having realized the true nature of reality as it abides—that very

body.text: skandheṣu piṇḍagrāha evātmagrahaṇahetuḥ, sa eva ca tathāgatasya piṇḍagrāho 'tigāḍhataraḥ syāt, tadaprahāṇaṃ cābhipretaṃ bhavet | na tvevam, ata evānyatra yo bālajanebhyaḥ piṇḍagrāha ātmagrāhasya hetutvena bhagavatā bhāṣitaḥ sa paramārthato 'grāhya eva | grāhye hi piṇḍe ekānekasvabhāvasya kasyacidabhāvāt | bālajanaprasiddho bhāvaḥ kevalaṃ saṃvṛtita uktaḥ | tenocyate piṇḍagrāha iti | tadarthasādhanāyaivaṃ bhagavān piṇḍagrāasyārthamuktavān | kimucyata iti cet? vyavahāre piṇḍagrāha iti paramārthe 'bhāvāt sa dharmastvanabhilāpya ityuktavān |
body.translated_text: Aggregate-grasping in the <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates) is indeed the cause of self-grasping; and that very aggregate-grasping of the <s>Tathāgata</s> would be exceedingly tenacious, and its non-abandonment would be intended. But that is not so. For this very reason, that which elsewhere has been spoken of by the <s>Bhagavān</s> to foolish persons as aggregate-grasping being the cause of self-grasping—that is ultimately ungraspable indeed. For in the graspable aggregate, no one-and-many nature whatsoever exists. What is well-known to foolish persons is merely stated conventionally. Therefore it is called "aggregate-grasping." For the purpose of establishing that meaning, the <s>Bhagavān</s> stated the meaning of aggregate-grasping in this way. If asked: what did he say? In conventional usage, "aggregate-grasping"—but since it is non-existent ultimately, that <s>dharma</s> is inexpressible—thus he said.

body.text: yadyevaṃ grāhyaḥ piṇḍo na syāt tadā tatra grāhakasyāpyabhāvāt kathaṃ vyavahāre piṇḍagrāha iti vicintyāha- sa ca bālapṛthajanairudgṛhītaḥ iti | bālāstu bhrāntivaśādasantamapi sadbhūtamiva gṛhaṇanti | tadāśayavaśena vyavahāraḥ prajñapyate, (ato) na virodha ityabhiprāyaḥ | tasmāt te bālā ityucyante, anyathā yathāvastu vyavahāraprajñaptau kathaṃ te bālāḥ syuḥ?
body.translated_text: If so, and the graspable aggregate does not exist, then since the grasper therein also would not exist, how is it "aggregate-grasping" in conventional usage?—reflecting thus, he says: "And that has been grasped by foolish ordinary persons." But the foolish, through the force of delusion, grasp even what is non-existent as though it were real. In accordance with that disposition, conventional usage is designated; therefore there is no contradiction—that is the purport. Therefore they are called "foolish"; otherwise, if conventional designation were in accordance with reality, how would they be foolish?

body.text: uktamatra kathaṃ cittaṃ pragrahītavyamiti | gāmbhīryamaudāryamapi cātra pūrvavad yojanīyam | anena yadā sarve bhāvāḥ paramārthataḥ svabhāvaśūnyāstadā rūpakāyaḥ jñānakāyaśca kathaṃ bhavet paramārthataḥ sasvabhāvaḥ, mūlasattvasyābhāvāditi deśitam |
body.translated_text: Here it has been stated how the mind should be uplifted. The profundity and vastness here should also be understood as before. By this, it has been taught: when all entities are ultimately devoid of intrinsic nature, how could the form-body (<s>rūpakāya</s>) or the knowledge-body (<s>jñānakāya</s>) be ultimately endowed with intrinsic nature, since the fundamental being (<s>mūlasattva</s>) [i.e., the self] is non-existent?

body.text: samprati yo hi kaścit subhūte ityādinā sarvasthāneṣu yogasamāpatteḥ kenopāyena sarvatra samādheyamiti tat pradarśyate | evamanusandhiḥ- yadi nāsti piṇḍagrāhastadā tanmūlaprabhavāyāḥ satkāyadṛṣṭerevābhāvāt kathaṃ bhagavān pañcasu dṛṣṭiṣu satkāyadṛṣṭimāheti tadarthaṃ yo hi kaścit subhūte ityādyāha | atra kathamavikalpyam, yaścāvikalpakaḥ, yaminnavikalpyam, yenāvikalpakaḥ, yaścāvikalpaḥ, taddarśanena yogasamāpatteḥ samyagupāyo darśito bhavati |
body.translated_text: Now, by 'If, <s>Subhūti</s>, anyone' and so forth, it is shown by what method meditative attainment (<s>yogasamāpatti</s>) should be established in all stations. The logical connection is as follows: if there is no grasping at aggregates (<s>piṇḍagrāha</s>), then, since even the view of the self-collection (<s>satkāyadṛṣṭi</s>) that arises from that root would be absent, how did the <s>Bhagavān</s> declare the view of the self-collection to be foremost among the five [wrong] views? For that purpose he says 'If, <s>Subhūti</s>, anyone' and so forth. Here, how is the non-conceptualized (<s>avikalpya</s>), who is the non-conceptualizer (<s>avikalpakaḥ</s>), with respect to what is there non-conceptualization, by what means is there non-conceptualization, and what is non-conceptualization — by showing these, the correct method of meditative attainment (<s>yogasamāpatti</s>) is demonstrated.

body.text: tatra yo hi kaścit subhūte ityārabhya tenocyate ātmadṛṣṭiḥ etatparyantamanena kathamavikalpyaṃ taduddiṣṭam | kathamiti cet? ukto 'nyairthikairātmā, bhagavatā tu pudgalanairātmyapratipādanādātmaniṣedhārthamāha ātmadṛṣṭiḥ iti tasyāḥ ātmadṛṣṭernirākaraṇena dharmanairātmyaṃ vyavasthāpyate adṛṣṭiḥ sā tathāgatena bhāṣitā ityuktam | tāmātmadṛṣṭiṃ yadi satyato na gṛhṇāti (tadā) evaṃ prayoge bodhisattvo yogasamāpattau pravartate | yasmādavikalpakastasmāt sa tatrāvaraṇopāyaḥ |
body.translated_text: There, beginning from 'If, <s>Subhūti</s>, anyone' up to 'therefore it is called self-view (<s>ātmadṛṣṭi</s>)' — by this, how the non-conceptualized is [to be understood] is indicated. How so? The self (<s>ātman</s>) has been asserted by other schools (<s>tīrthika</s>); but the <s>Bhagavān</s>, for the purpose of negating the self through establishing the selflessness of persons (<s>pudgalanairātmya</s>), says 'self-view' (<s>ātmadṛṣṭi</s>). By the rejection of that self-view, the selflessness of <s>dharmas</s> (<s>dharmanairātmya</s>) is established — [thus] it was said: 'that view is spoken of by the <s>Tathāgata</s> as a non-view.' If one does not grasp that self-view as real, then in such a practice the <s>bodhisattva</s> engages in meditative attainment (<s>yogasamāpatti</s>). Since he is non-conceptualizing, that is the method for [removing] obscurations there.

body.text: evaṃ hi subhūtea bodhisattvayānasamprasthitena ityanena yo 'vikalpakaḥ sa paridīpyate | sarvadharmāḥ ityanena yasminnavikalpyam taddarśitam | jñātavyā draṣṭavyā adhimoktavyāḥ ityanena yenāvikalpyaṃ tadabhihitam | kenāvikalpyamitiṃ cet? jñānena darśanena adhimuktyā ca | tatra jñānaṃ śrutamayī prajñā, darśanaṃ cintāyayī prajñā, tayopanidhyānatvād, adhimuktiḥ bhāvanāmayī prajñā, adhyāśayo 'trādhimuktiśabdena vaktumiṣyate | sā tu bhāvanābalena sidhyatīti, ata eva bhāvanamayī prajñā nirvedhabhāgīyāvasthāyāmadhimuktiśabdenoktā |
body.translated_text: By 'Thus indeed, <s>Subhūti</s>, one who has set out in the <s>Bodhisattva</s> vehicle,' who the non-conceptualizer is, is illuminated. By 'all <s>dharmas</s>,' with respect to what there is non-conceptualization is shown. By 'should be known, should be seen, should be resolved upon,' by what means there is non-conceptualization is stated. By what is there non-conceptualization? By knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>), by seeing (<s>darśana</s>), and by resolution (<s>adhimukti</s>). Of these, knowledge is the wisdom born of hearing (<s>śrutamayī prajñā</s>); seeing is the wisdom born of reflection (<s>cintāmayī prajñā</s>), because of its close examination; resolution is the wisdom born of meditation (<s>bhāvanāmayī prajñā</s>) — by the word 'resolution' (<s>adhimukti</s>), superior intention (<s>adhyāśaya</s>) is intended. That is accomplished through the power of meditation; therefore, the wisdom born of meditation in the preparatory stage (<s>nirvedhabhāgīyāvasthā</s>) is called by the word 'resolution.'

body.text: tathā cādhimoktavyā, yathā na pratyupasthāmahe ityanena yo 'vikalpastaṃ darśayati | asaṃjñaiṣā tathāgatena bhāṣitā ityatra hetuḥ parikīrtitaḥ | kasyacit saṃjñeyasya abhāvo 'pi, ekānekasvabhāvaśūnyatvāt paramārthata sā asaṃjñā | saṃvṛtisatyamadhikṛtyānyatra tathāgatena bhāṣitam | tasyā (

children.translated_text: <s>Vajraṭ</s> 223

children.text: ) mithyārthādhigamāvasthāyāṃ kathaṃ na syādavikalpa ityabhiprāyaḥ | sarvasthāneṣu yogasamāpattyupāyo 'bhihitaḥ |
children.translated_text: in the state of comprehending the false meaning, how could there not be non-conceptualization? — this is the intent. The method of meditative attainment (<s>yogasamāpatti</s>) across all stations has been stated.

body.translated_text: And one should so resolve that 'one does not stand before them' (<s>na pratyupasthāmahe</s>) — by this, what non-conceptualization is, is shown. 'That is spoken of by the <s>Tathāgata</s> as a non-perception (<s>asaṃjñā</s>)' — here the reason is declared. Even the absence of any object of perception — because it is ultimately empty of the nature of unity or multiplicity — that is a non-perception. The <s>Tathāgata</s> has spoken otherwise [only] with reference to conventional truth (<s>saṃvṛtisatya</s>). Of that,

body.text: 3. asaṃkleśena prasthitiḥ (a) deśanāsaṃkleśaḥ
body.translated_text: 3. Progress without defilement (<s>asaṃkleśa</s>). (a) Non-defilement in teaching (<s>deśanāsaṃkleśa</s>).

body.text: dvidhā tavadasaṅkleśaḥ- deśanāsaṃkleśaḥ, saṃsārāsaṃkleśaśca | tatra yadi nāsti dharmasaṃjñā tadā tathāgatasya sattvebhyo taddharmadeśanāsaṃjñāsamutpāde kathaṃ na bhavet saṃkleśaḥ? kṛpayā sattvārthaṃ yāvatsaṃsārāvasthāne sati dharmasaṃjñayā kathaṃ na syāt saṃkleśaḥ? iti vicintya tayaiva cittasampadā deśanāsaṃkleśaṃ gāthayā ca saṃsārākleśamāvedayitum yaśca khalu punaḥ subhūte ityādyāha |
body.translated_text: Non-defilement is twofold: non-defilement in teaching (<s>deśanāsaṃkleśa</s>) and non-defilement in <s>saṃsāra</s> (<s>saṃsārāsaṃkleśa</s>). Regarding the first: if there is no perception of <s>dharma</s> (<s>dharmasaṃjñā</s>), then when the perception of teaching the <s>Dharma</s> to beings arises in the <s>Tathāgata</s>, how would there not be defilement? When, out of compassion, for the benefit of beings, while remaining in <s>saṃsāra</s>, there is a perception of <s>dharma</s> — how would there not be defilement? Reflecting thus, to declare the non-defilement in teaching through that very mental accomplishment, and to indicate the non-defilement in <s>saṃsāra</s> through a verse, he says 'And again, <s>Subhūti</s>' and so forth.

body.text: pūrvaṃ prasaṅgāntare lokadhātupraśastipradarśanamanuśaṃsāyāḥ praśaṃsanam, sampratyasaṃkleśādhikāre 'nantalokadhātudeśanayā nocyate anuśaṃseti na punaruktiḥ | atrāpi yuktistu prāgvad vaktavyā | udgṛhya iti svadhyāye 'dhītam, dhārayet iti padam, vācayet iti pustakāsikaṃ vācayet, paryavāpnuyāt iti tvarthagrahaṇamityarthaḥ | anena yamānmahārtho 'yaṃ dharmastasmādbodhisattvenaivaṃvidhāyāṃ mahārthadharmadeśanāyāmavaśyameva chanda-praṇidhānābhyāṃ sthātavyaṃ tatparidīpitam |
body.translated_text: Previously, in a different context, the praise of world-systems was a demonstration of the benefits and a commendation. Now, in the topic of non-defilement, through the teaching of infinite world-systems, it is not said to be [merely] a benefit — hence there is no repetition. The reasoning here too should be stated as before. 'Having memorized' (<s>udgṛhya</s>) means having studied through self-study (<s>svādhyāya</s>); 'would retain' (<s>dhārayet</s>) means the words; 'would recite' (<s>vācayet</s>) means would recite from a manuscript; 'would comprehend' (<s>paryavāpnuyāt</s>) means would grasp the meaning. By this, it is illuminated that since this <s>Dharma</s> is of such great significance, a <s>bodhisattva</s> must necessarily abide in aspiration (<s>chanda</s>) and resolve (<s>praṇidhāna</s>) for the teaching of such greatly significant <s>Dharma</s>.

body.text: bhāṣyamāṇāyāmapi kathaṃ na syātsaṃkleśa ityetaddarśayituṃ kathaṃ na samprakāśayet ityāha | ayamabhiprāyaḥ- paramārthato 'nutpannatvenabhilāpyatvena deśitatve 'pi sarvadharmāṇām, te dharmā anabhilāpyasvabhāvena nocyate | evamuktam- yathā vineyajanāstathā sarve dharmā ādito 'nutpannatvādanabhilāpyāḥ (

children.translated_text: <s>Vajraṭ</s> 224

children.text: ) tasmānna te kenāpi vyapadeśyā ityevaṃ darśyata iti | tathā sati asaṃkleśena deśanā, aviparītārthatvāt | anyathā saṃkliṣṭā syād viparītadeśanatvāt | ata eva tathāgato dharmadeśanākāle viśuddhalokajñāne prasthitaḥ, ato dharmasaṃjñābhāsasamudbhave 'pi tattvato 'bhiniveśābhāvāt saṃkleśadoṣābhāvaḥ | anena yogasamāpattiḥ, cittapragrahaḥ gāmbhīryañca nirdiṣṭam, pūrveṇa tāvadaudāryam |
children.translated_text: Therefore they are not to be designated by anyone' — thus it is shown. That being the case, the teaching is without defilement, because it is of non-inverted meaning. Otherwise, it would be defiled, because it would be an inverted teaching. Therefore, the <s>Tathāgata</s>, at the time of teaching the <s>Dharma</s>, is established in purified world-knowledge; therefore, even when the appearance of a <s>dharma</s>-perception arises, because there is no attachment to it in reality, there is no fault of defilement. By this, meditative attainment (<s>yogasamāpatti</s>), taking hold of the mind (<s>cittapragraha</s>), and profundity (<s>gāmbhīrya</s>) are indicated; by the former, magnificence (<s>audārya</s>) [is indicated].

body.translated_text: To show how, even when [the Dharma] is being spoken, there would be no defilement, he says 'How should one illuminate [it]?' This is the intent: although all <s>dharmas</s> are taught, since they are ultimately unoriginated and therefore inexpressible, those <s>dharmas</s> are not spoken of through their inexpressible nature. Thus it is said: 'Just as beings to be trained, so all <s>dharmas</s>, being unoriginated from the beginning, are inexpressible.

body.text: ba
body.translated_text: (b) Non-defilement in <s>saṃsāra</s> (<s>saṃsārāsaṃkleśa</s>).

body.text: saṃsārāsaṃkleśaḥ

sāmprataṃ nikhilaprajñāpāramitākāyaṃ vyavasthāpya gāthayā saṃsārāsaṃkleśo deśyate | anayā gāthayā catvāri saṃskṛtalakṣaṇāni paridīpitāni | (tāni tāvat) svabhāvalakṣaṇam, viṣayarasāsvādanalakṣaṇam, ādīnavānvayalakṣaṇam, niryāṇānvayalakṣaṇaṃ ceti |
body.translated_text: Now, having established the entire body of the <s>Prajñāpāramitā</s>, the non-defilement in <s>saṃsāra</s> is taught through a verse. By this verse, the four characteristics of the conditioned (<s>saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa</s>) are illuminated. They are: (1) the characteristic of intrinsic nature (<s>svabhāvalakṣaṇa</s>), (2) the characteristic of relishing sense-objects (<s>viṣayarasāsvādanalakṣaṇa</s>), (3) the characteristic connected with danger (<s>ādīnavānvayalakṣaṇa</s>), and (4) the characteristic connected with escape (<s>niryāṇānvayalakṣaṇa</s>).

body.text: tatra pañcaskandhātmakānāṃ bhāvānāṃ yathāpratīti pratītyasamutpādastāvad hetupratyayasaṃgṛhitatvāt saṃskṛtaṃ ityucyate | eteṣāṃ sarveṣāṃ svabhāvaḥ tārakāḥ iva draṣṭavyaḥ | rātrau yathā tārakā avabhāsante, na tu divase, tathaiva saṃskṛtā api avidyājñānāndhakāre sati pratibhāsante, jñānasūryāloke sati nāvabhāsante, ataḥ (te) tārakasvabhāvā iva draṣṭavyāḥ | pudgaladharmadṛṣṭayabhiniveśātmakāḥ saṃskṛtāstu mithyāpratītihetutvāt timiravajjñātavyāḥ |
body.translated_text: Among these, the dependent origination (<s>pratītyasamutpāda</s>) of entities consisting of the five aggregates (<s>pañcaskandha</s>), as they are perceived, is called 'conditioned' (<s>saṃskṛta</s>) because it is comprised of causes and conditions (<s>hetupratyaya</s>). The intrinsic nature of all these should be viewed as like stars (<s>tārakā</s>). Just as stars shine at night but not during the day, so too conditioned things appear when there is the darkness of ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), but do not appear when there is the sunlight of knowledge (<s>jñāna</s>) — therefore they should be viewed as being of the nature of stars. Conditioned things consisting of attachment to the views of self and <s>dharmas</s> (<s>pudgaladharma-dṛṣṭyabhiniveśa</s>) should be understood as like a visual aberration (<s>timira</s>), because they are the cause of false perception.

body.text: vijñānalakṣaṇaṃ ca karmavartikaṃ tṛṣṇāsnehaṃ cāśritya prajvalanād dāpa iva draṣṭavyam, evametannidarśanena saṃskṛtasvabhāvalakṣaṇaṃ paridīpitam | māyopamayā viṣayarasāsvādanalakṣaṇaṃ nirdiśyate, vitathāvabhāsamānatvāt | tatrādīnavānvayalakṣaṇaṃ saṃskṛtasvabhāvaṃ dvividham- anityānvayaḥ duḥkhānvayaśca | avaśyāyopamayā anityatānvayaḥ pradarśyate, na ciraṃ sthitatvāt | budbudopamayā tāvad (

children.translated_text: <s>Vajraṭ</s> 225

children.text: ) duḥkhatānvayaḥ pradarśyate, vedanā budbudopamā iti, yā kācid vedanā seha duḥkhamiti bhāṣitatvāt |
children.translated_text: the connection with suffering is demonstrated — 'feelings are like bubbles,' since it has been stated that 'whatever feeling there is, that is suffering here.'

body.translated_text: The characteristic of consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>), depending on the mechanism of <s>karma</s> and the fuel of craving (<s>tṛṣṇā</s>), should be viewed as like a lamp (<s>dīpa</s>), because it blazes forth. Thus, by these illustrations, the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of the conditioned is illuminated. By the simile of illusion (<s>māyā</s>), the characteristic of relishing sense-objects is indicated — because they appear falsely. Among these, the characteristic connected with danger (<s>ādīnavānvaya</s>) of the conditioned nature is twofold: connected with impermanence (<s>anityānvaya</s>) and connected with suffering (<s>duḥkhānvaya</s>). By the simile of dewdrops (<s>avaśyāya</s>), the connection with impermanence is demonstrated — because they do not endure long. By the simile of bubbles (<s>budbuda</s>),

body.text: trividhaiḥ dukhaiḥ sarvā vedanā duḥkhā veditavyā | tatra duḥkhavedanā tāvad duḥkhaduḥkham, tatsahitā ye saṃskārāste 'pi tadanurūpatayā duḥkhameva; sukhāvedanā tāvad vipariṇāmaduḥkhena duḥkham, tatsahitā ye dharmāste 'pi tadanurūpatayā duḥkham, na duḥkhā na sukhā vedanā, tatsahitāni vastūni ca saṃskāraduḥkham, utpādabhaṅgalakṣaṇatvena tāni duḥkham | evaṃ sarvaṃ saṃskṛtaṃ duḥkhānvitaṃ draṣṭavyam |
body.translated_text: All feelings should be understood as suffering through the three types of suffering. Among these, painful feeling is the suffering of suffering (<s>duḥkhaduḥkha</s>); the conditioned things (<s>saṃskāras</s>) associated with it, being of corresponding nature, are also suffering. Pleasant feeling is suffering through the suffering of change (<s>vipariṇāmaduḥkha</s>); the <s>dharmas</s> associated with it, being of corresponding nature, are also suffering. The feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant, and the things associated with it, constitute the suffering of conditioned existence (<s>saṃskāraduḥkha</s>) — because they are characterized by arising and perishing, they are suffering. Thus, all that is conditioned should be viewed as pervaded by suffering.

body.text: tatra niryāṇānvayalakṣaṇaṃ tāvat pudgaladharmaśūnyatānvayam, tadālambananirvṛtatvādbhagavatā khalu dvividhaṃniryāṇālambanamuktam | āryasamādhirājasūtrecāpyuktam :
body.translated_text: Among these, the characteristic connected with escape (<s>niryāṇānvayalakṣaṇa</s>) is connected with the emptiness of persons and <s>dharmas</s> (<s>pudgaladharmaśūnyatā</s>), since <s>nirvāṇa</s> is achieved through taking that [emptiness] as its object. Indeed, the <s>Bhagavān</s> has spoken of a twofold basis of escape (<s>niryāṇālambana</s>). And in the <s>Āryasamādhirājasūtra</s> too it is said:

children.translated_text: 'If one examines the <s>dharmas</s> of selflessness (<s>nairātmya</s>),
and having examined them, if one meditates [upon them],
that is the cause for attaining the fruit of <s>nirvāṇa</s>;
no other cause leads to peace.'

body.text: dvividhanairātmyasamprayuktāḥ sarvasaṃskṛtāḥ, tathā hi- atīta-pratyutpanna-anāgatabhedena trividhāḥ saṃskṛtāḥ | tatra ye tāvadatītāste smṛtimātrāvasthitā ato niḥsvabhāvatvena, dharma-pudgalatayā śūnyāḥ ātmanānadhiṣṭhitatvāt, tataśca svapnaupamyena dvividhanairātmyānvayāste vyapadiṣṭāḥ | pratyupannā vidyudaupamyena ekānekasvabhāvarahitāḥ agrāhyasvabhāvatvaditi tenānvitā vyapadiṣṭāḥ | (

children.translated_text: <s>Vajraṭ</s> 226

children.text: ) anāgatāstāvadalabdhasvabhāvāḥ, abhraupamyena ākāśasamacitte tadbījadauṣṭhulyena janitatvāditi nairātmyadvayaṃ tāvaddeśitam |
children.translated_text: Those in the future, being of yet-unattained nature, by the simile of a cloud (<s>abhra</s>) — because they are produced by the seed and predisposition [of <s>karma</s>] in a mind that is like space — thus the twofold selflessness is taught.

body.translated_text: All conditioned things are connected with the twofold selflessness (<s>nairātmyadvaya</s>). For conditioned things are threefold through the division of past, present, and future. Among these, those that are past subsist only as memory; therefore, being devoid of intrinsic nature, they are empty as <s>dharmas</s> and as persons, since they are not sustained by a self. Hence, by the simile of a dream (<s>svapna</s>), they are designated as connected with the twofold selflessness. Those in the present, by the simile of lightning (<s>vidyut</s>), being devoid of the nature of unity or multiplicity, being of an ungraspable nature — they are designated as connected with that [twofold selflessness].

body.text: ato 'nena khalu samagreṇātra bodhisattvaiḥ sadā sarvasaṃskṛtasvabhāvamevaṃ vicārya chanda-praṇidhānābhyāṃ sthātavyamiti paridīpitam | niryāṇānvapradarśanena tāvad yogasamāpattiścittapragrahaśca nirdiṣṭaḥ | anena sampūrṇenasthānena gāmbhīryañca vyapadiṣṭam |
body.translated_text: Therefore, by this in its entirety, it is illuminated that <s>bodhisattvas</s> should always examine the nature of all conditioned things (<s>saṃskṛta</s>) in this manner and abide through aspiration (<s>chanda</s>) and vow (<s>praṇidhāna</s>). By the demonstration of the way of deliverance (<s>niryāṇa</s>), meditative attainment (<s>yogasamāpatti</s>) and the uplift of the mind (<s>cittapragraha</s>) are indicated. By this complete section, the profundity (<s>gāmbhīrya</s>) is also indicated.

body.text: gāthāyāmasyāṃ tāvadidaṃ paridīpyate- saṃkleśamulaṃ tāvad viparyāsaḥ | ataḥ saṃskṛtasvabhāveṣvanekaśaḥ kenacid vicārayatā manasikurvatā apyevaṃ saṃskāraparijñānādyadā viparyāsābhāvāt na bhavati saṃkleśaṃ (tadā) kathaṃ (nāma) yathāvadaśesavastusvabhāvaparibhāvako vidhūtāśeṣaviparyāsajālastathāgataḥ saṃkliṣṭo bhavet | ata eva samastasaṃskṛtadoṣān avagacchan tathāgataḥ, padmamiva saṃsāradoṣāmbhasānavaliptacittaḥ, pratijñātasamastajagatsamuddharaṇāśayaḥ, saphalakāritraḥ, mahākaruṇānvitacittaḥ, niravadhijagaddhitasukhasādhanābhiprāyeṇa saṃsāracakrasaṃsaraṇaṃ yāvat pratiṣṭhito veditavyaḥ | tathā coktam-
body.translated_text: In this verse, the following is illuminated: The root of affliction (<s>saṃkleśa</s>) is indeed perversion (<s>viparyāsa</s>). Therefore, when someone, having examined and attended to the nature of conditioned things in many ways, through the full comprehension of formations (<s>saṃskāraparijñāna</s>), no longer has perversion and hence no affliction — how then could the <s>Tathāgata</s>, who contemplates the nature of all entities as they truly are and who has shaken off the entire net of perversions, become afflicted? For this very reason, the <s>Tathāgata</s>, comprehending all the faults of the conditioned, with a mind unstained by the waters of <s>saṃsāra</s>'s faults like a lotus, whose intention is to rescue all beings as he has vowed, whose conduct bears fruit, whose mind is endowed with great compassion (<s>mahākaruṇā</s>), should be understood as established in the turning of the wheel of <s>saṃsāra</s> with the intent of accomplishing the benefit and happiness of beings without limit. And thus it has been said:

body.text: kartuṃ loke sukhaṃ śāntau bhave cāpyanadhiṣṭhitaḥ | iti sarvasattvānavalokituṃ bhūmāvasthīyata ityapyuktam |
body.translated_text: 'To bring happiness to the world, in peace, and yet not established in [mere] existence' — thus it is also said that 'he remains on the [bodhisattva] stages in order to look upon all sentient beings.'

children.text: traiyadhvikānāṃ jananī munīnāṃ khyātā yathāśakti mayā tato jagat |
children.translated_text: She who is renowned as the mother of the sages of the three times — as far as I am able, [I have explained her]. Therefore, may the world,

children.text: vipulena puṇyena viyatsamena vidhūya cāndhyaṃ sugatatvamāpnuyāt ||
children.translated_text: through the vast merit equal to space, having dispelled its blindness, attain the state of a <s>Sugata</s> (Well-gone One, i.e., Buddha)!

body.text: ācāryakamalaśīlena mādhyamikanayena viracitā vistṛtā āryavajracchedikāṭīkā parisamāptā | aṣṭamyāṃ śatābdyāṃ bhāratīyācārya mañjuśrīmitreṇa bhota-locāvā yeśe-demahābhāgena ca bhoṭabhāṣāyāmanūditā | viduṣāṃ vaśaṃvadena ācāryapemātenajinamahādayena bhoṭabhāṣātaḥ saṃskṛtabhāṣāyāṃ punaruddhṛtā sarvasattvahitasukhārtham iti |
body.translated_text: The extensive commentary on the noble <s>Vajracchedikā</s> (<s>Āryavajracchedikāṭīkā</s>), composed by the master <s>Kamalaśīla</s> according to the <s>Mādhyamika</s> system, is complete. In the eighth century, it was translated into the Tibetan language by the Indian master <s>Mañjuśrīmitra</s> and the great Tibetan translator <s>Ye-shes-sde</s>. It was retranslated from the Tibetan language into Sanskrit by the master <s>Pemātena Jinamahādaya</s>, who was at the service of scholars, for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings.
